questions.q: Where do LWC component unit tests actually run?
options: Inside a live Salesforce Developer Edition org, through the browser
Inside the Salesforce CLI's deployment pipeline only, never locally
Entirely outside of Salesforce, in a local or CI JavaScript environment powered by Jest
Inside the Lightning App Builder preview pane
questions.explain: LWC tests run entirely outside a Salesforce org, in Jest, using @salesforce/sfdx-lwc-jest to provide Salesforce-specific mocks -- making them fast and usable in CI without a live org or network connection.

questions.q: What does `createElement('c-hello-world', { is: HelloWorld })` do in a test?
options: It deploys the component to a scratch org for testing
It is a Jest matcher used only for assertions, not component creation
It renders the component immediately without needing to append it anywhere
It creates an instance of the component for testing, given its tag name and the imported class
questions.explain: createElement, imported from the lwc module, creates a testable instance of the component using its tag name and the is option pointing to the imported class -- step one of the standard test pattern.

questions.q: Why must a test query rendered content through `element.shadowRoot.querySelector(...)` rather than `document.querySelector(...)`?
options: document.querySelector is deprecated and no longer works in Jest
shadowRoot is only available in test environments, not in real browsers
The component renders into its own shadow DOM, the same encapsulation boundary that applies in a real app -- document-level queries can't reach inside it
There is no real difference; either query works identically
questions.explain: The same shadow DOM encapsulation that applies in a running app applies inside tests -- querying through element.shadowRoot is required to reach content rendered inside the component's own shadow tree.

questions.q: Why does a test that sets an @api property and then checks the rendered result often need a pattern like `Promise.resolve().then(...)` before asserting?
options: Because rendering isn't always synchronous with a property assignment, so a microtask tick is needed to let the framework finish rendering before the assertion runs
Because Jest requires every test to return a Promise, regardless of what's being tested
Because @api properties can only be read inside a Promise callback
Because createElement is itself asynchronous and never resolves synchronously
questions.explain: A property assignment doesn't necessarily trigger a synchronous re-render -- waiting a microtask tick via Promise.resolve().then(...) gives the framework time to finish rendering before the test asserts on the result.

questions.q: What is the purpose of clearing `document.body` in an `afterEach` block across LWC Jest tests?
options: It is purely optional styling cleanup with no effect on test correctness
It is required only when testing components that use @wire
It resets the Salesforce org's data between test runs
Without it, elements from one test can linger into the next, causing querySelector to match the wrong element or tests to interfere with each other
questions.explain: Leftover elements in document.body from a prior test can cause later tests to accidentally query stale elements or otherwise interfere with each other -- which is why this cleanup is close to mandatory boilerplate.
